ctDiscretePars

Source: R/ctDiscretePars.R
ctDiscretePars.Rd

Calculate model implied regressions for a sequence of time intervals (if ct) or steps (if dt) based on a ctStanFit object, for specified subjects. Wrap with print() when used inside for loops! ctStanDiscretePars is maintained as a backward-compatible alias.

Usage

ctDiscretePars(
  fit,
  subjects = "popmean",
  times = seq(from = 0, to = 10, by = 0.1),
  nsamples = 200,
  impulseType = "unit",
  standardise = FALSE,
  cov = FALSE,
  plot = FALSE,
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 2L),
  state = NULL,
  method = "linearise",
  realid = TRUE,
  ...,
  ctstanfitobj,
  observational
)

Arguments

fit

model fit from ctFit

subjects

Either 'popmean', to use the population mean parameter, or the subjects to use, as ids in the data (see realid).

times

Numeric vector of positive values, discrete time parameters will be calculated for each. If the fit object is a discrete time model, these should be positive integers.

nsamples

Number of samples from the stanfit to use for plotting. Higher values will increase smoothness / accuracy, at cost of plotting speed. Values greater than the total number of samples will be set to total samples.

impulseType

What a "one unit change in process c" brings with it. Each option gives dtDRIFT(t) %*% C for a different matrix C, whose column c says what else changes.

'unit' (the default)

C = I. Process c alone changes by one unit (one standard deviation when standardise=TRUE). This is the partial regression E[x(t+u)|x(t)], and the only option that depends on the dynamics alone.

'observed'

C = Sigma diag(Sigma)^-1 with Sigma = asymDIFFUSIONcov. Process c is observed one unit above its expectation, and the other processes change with it by Sigma_rc/Sigma_cc. This is the simple regression, the one obtained by regressing the observed data on x_c alone.

'shock'

C = Q diag(Q)^-1 with Q = DIFFUSIONcov. A system noise innovation in c, with the correlated innovations Q_rc/Q_cc in the other processes. This is an impulse response.

'orthogonal'

From the Cholesky factor of DIFFUSION, so shocks are uncorrelated. The result depends on the order of the latent processes.

These matrices are not symmetric: a one unit change in a process with a large variance implies a larger change in one with a small variance than the reverse. 'observed' and 'shock' are the same only when every process decays at the same rate and there are no cross effects.

standardise

Logical, FALSE by default. If TRUE, report the effect of a one standard deviation change in process c in standard deviations of process r, with both taken from the stationary within subject covariance asymDIFFUSIONcov. This makes effects between processes on different scales comparable, and is what ctNetwork reports by default. With FALSE the effects are in the processes' own units, and impulseType='unit', standardise=FALSE gives expm(DRIFT*t). Draws for a system with no stationary variance are returned as NaN, with a message. The plot title states which scale was used.

cov

Logical. If TRUE, covariances are returned instead of regression coefficients.

plot

Logical. If TRUE, ggplots output using ctDiscreteParsPlot instead of returning output.

cores

Number of cpu cores to use for computing subject matrices. If subject matrices were saved during fiting, not used.

state

Where to evaluate matrix cells that depend on the latent state or a time dependent predictor (see ctContextDependence). NULL (the default) or 'T0MEANS' uses the population initial state, with time dependent predictors at zero. For a model whose dynamics depend on the state this can be far from the data. 'mean' uses the mean smoothed latent state, 'asymptotic' the system's fixed point, and a numeric vector gives the state directly. The initial state and the fixed point are computed for each posterior draw, so their uncertainty is included in the intervals. 'mean' uses the estimate's mean state for every draw, so its uncertainty is not included. A process that does not change (a latent predictor) is held at its initial value when finding the fixed point. Requires backend='julia' and subjects='popmean'. For a linear model the argument has no effect.

method

How the regressions are computed. 'linearise' (the default) computes expm(J*t), with J the Jacobian of the drift (the model's JAx) at the evaluation point. For a linear model J is the DRIFT matrix and the result is exact. For a model whose dynamics depend on the state, J can differ from DRIFT: a DRIFT cell a + b*Y in the column of process Y contributes a + 2*b*Y to the Jacobian. A stan fit has no Jacobian, and uses DRIFT evaluated at T0MEANS. The linearisation is accurate near a fixed point and for intervals that are short relative to the dynamics. 'simulate' integrates the nonlinear system from state, and from state plus a shock of one stationary standard deviation in each process in turn (with the accompanying changes impulseType gives), and takes the difference between the trajectories, scaled to one unit (one standard deviation when standardise=TRUE). It gives the same result as 'linearise' when no cell depends on the state. For a strongly nonlinear system the result depends on the size of the shock. 'simulate' requires backend='julia' and is slower, so it uses nsamples posterior draws, with a small default.

realid

If TRUE (the default), subjects are read as the ids in the data, and integers that are not ids there are read as ctsem's numbering of the subjects, 1 to N, with a message. If FALSE, they are read as that numbering.

...

additional plotting arguments to control ctDiscreteParsPlot

ctstanfitobj

Deprecated. Use fit.

observational

Deprecated. Use impulseType: FALSE is 'unit' and TRUE is 'observed'.

Value

With plot = FALSE, an array of class ctDiscretePars holding the discrete time coefficients, by sample, subject, time interval, row and column. summary() (summary.ctDiscretePars) gives each curve's peak, the time of the peak, the time at which it falls to half the peak (a half-life), and the area under it, with their uncertainty. For an optimised fit with subjects = 'popmean', the coefficients at the fit's estimate are in attr(x, 'estimate'), by subject, time interval, row and column. These are computed from the matrices ctSummaryMatrices(fit, state = )$estimate reports, or for 'simulate' simulated at the estimate, and can differ from the mean or median of the draws. summary() reports them in an estimate column, and ctDiscreteParsPlot draws them as its line. Sampled fits, and subjects other than 'popmean', have no such estimate. With plot = TRUE, a ggplot object.

Details

impulseType='unit' with standardise=FALSE gives the discrete time autoregressive and cross-lagged matrix, expm(DRIFT*t). impulseType='observed' with standardise=TRUE gives the model implied cross-correlation function, Cor(x_r(t+u), x_c(t)), which corresponds to the empirical autocorrelations ctACF computes from the data, and equals the latent correlation matrix at t=0.

If plot=TRUE, the function will return a ggplot2 object (and hence needs to be printed if intended to display within a loop). This can be modified by the various ggplot2 functions, or displayed using print(x).

Examples

data.table::setDTthreads(1) #ignore this line
ctDiscretePars(ctstantestfit,times=seq(.5,4,.1),
 plot=TRUE,indices='CR')

#modify plot
require(ggplot2)
g=ctDiscretePars(ctstantestfit,times=seq(.5,4,.1),
 plot=TRUE,indices='CR')
g= g+ labs(title='Cross effects')
print(g)
